title: Tajwid, a first taste
hookLine: recitation has rules of sound: stretching, nasal hums, stops
carry: every letter is due its right

cards: Put on a recording of the Qur'an recited well, and listen for a minute without trying to understand a word. It isn't quite singing, and it isn't quite speaking. Some vowels stretch, long and steady, like a held note.
Some sounds hum in the nose for a beat. Then the voice stops, exactly, breathes, and starts again. It sounds free, but it isn't improvised.
Every stretch and hum follows a rule, and tradition says the rules have been handed down teacher to student, by ear, the way a child in a mosque class still learns them.

teach.b: Tajwid comes from the root j-w-d, to make good, to make excellent; jayyid, good, is from the same root. So tajwid is making the recitation good: giving the words the sound they were given in.

Tajwid manuals, tradition says, define it with a line that became our carry: giving every letter its right and its due. Its right is how it's made: where in the throat, the tongue, the lips or the nose each letter lives.
Its due is what happens to it next to other letters. Three rules make a first taste.
One, madd, stretching. A long vowel is held for two beats, and in some places four or six. At the end of the Fatiha, wa lad-daaaallin, that long a is held for six.
Two, ghunnah, the nasal hum. When a noon or a meem is doubled, as in inna, the sound rests in the nose for two beats.
Three, waqf, stopping. Small marks above the line show where a stop is required, where it's allowed, and where stopping would bend the meaning.

teach.h: EVERY LETTER IS DUE ITS RIGHT.
teach.b: The Qur'an itself asks for this care: in Surah al-Muzzammil, recite the Qur'an with tartil, measured and distinct.
Scholars say avoiding mistakes that change meaning is required; the finer rules are a craft, learned by ear from a teacher, often with a chain of teachers going back generations.

And the kindest hadith for beginners: Bukhari and Muslim record the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ saying that the one skilled in the Qur'an is with the noble, righteous scribes, and the one who stumbles through it, finding it hard, gets two rewards.

how: Muslims learn tajwid from a teacher, usually by ear and repetition, often in mosque classes or with a local reciter; advanced students may receive an ijazah, a license to teach recitation, with a chain of teachers going back many generations.

games.q: you're learning to recite and keep stumbling on the letters. what does the hadith say about you?
o: better not to recite until you're fluent
games.why: the one who finds it hard and stumbles gets two rewards (Bukhari; Muslim). the struggle is counted.

practice: Say the word Allah slowly, in your mind or aloud if you're alone, and let the long a in the middle stretch for two beats. Then hum, mmm, lips closed, and feel where it sits, in the nose, behind the face: that's where ghunnah lives.
Then stop completely, let the silence be exact, and go round a few times: stretch, hum, stop.

wordCard.voice: Tajwid. Making excellent: the rules of Qur'an recitation, the stretch, the hum and the stop, so every letter gets its right. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: making excellent, from j-w-d; the rules of Qur'an recitation.

carryVoice: Your line: every letter is due its right. Every sound, given its full length. That's day two hundred twenty-eight.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4937; Sahih Muslim 798 (the skilled reciter and the one who stumbles)
